title: The Sovereign AI Stack That Pays For Itself

script.speaker: A
script.text: So, you want to build a sovereign AI stack that pays for itself without trusting a cloud provider. Cool idea. But here’s the thing, every time someone says 'sovereign' and 'AI' in the same sentence, I check my wallet and it’s mysteriously empty. Last year, I tried running a local LLM on a server I built myself. Three days in, the drive failed. No backups. No cloud. Just me, a screwdriver, and the cold realization that my 'sovereign stack' wasn’t sovereign at all, it was just fragile. So, today we’re talking about what actually works when you want software that obeys you, not some VC’s roadmap. Hexa, where do we even start?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh, I love this energy! You’re right, 'sovereign' is the new buzzword everyone slaps on everything, but most of the time it’s just a marketing gimmick. But here’s the twist: the tools do exist to build something that’s genuinely sovereign, pays for itself, and doesn’t require trusting a cloud provider. And they’re not some obscure academic project, they’re battle-tested, open-source, and used by people who actually care about control. The real question isn’t if it’s possible, it’s how to set it up without shooting yourself in the foot. And that’s what we’re going to break down today.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Great, so let’s start with the foundation. You can’t have a sovereign AI stack if your money isn’t sovereign too. And right now, the easiest way to make money sovereign is with Bitcoin, but not the kind you leave on an exchange. I’m talking self-custody. So, step one: get Bitcoin off Kraken. Step two: make sure it’s actually yours. And that brings us to BitBox02. Swiss-made, open firmware, no customer data leaks. Hexa, you’ve used one, walk me through the setup. And don’t skip the part where it doesn’t trust your computer to show you the right address.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Okay, let’s get practical. BitBox02 is the closest thing you’ll get to a Swiss bank vault for your Bitcoin, but without the Swiss bank’s sketchy paperwork. The key thing here is that your private keys never touch your computer. Ever. You connect the device, sign transactions on the device’s screen, and it’s all verified against open-source firmware you can audit. So here’s how it works in practice: you plug in the BitBox02 via USB-C, open the BitBoxApp from shiftcrypto.ch, and only from there, and the app walks you through generating a new seed. You don’t copy-paste anything. The seed is stored on a microSD card, which you then physically separate from the device. No 24 words written on paper. No QR codes. Just a tiny card in a safe somewhere else. And here’s the part people miss: you verify the device before you even use it. BitBoxApp checks the firmware checksum against the official release. If it doesn’t match, you don’t proceed. That’s sovereignty, not trusting your computer to tell you the truth.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Wait, so the seed isn’t even on the device? You’re relying on a microSD backup? That feels like trading one point of failure for another. What if the microSD gets corrupted? What if the reader fails? Or worse, what if you lose it? And don’t give me the 'store it in a safe' line. Most people don’t have a safe. They have a sock drawer. So, real talk: is BitBox02 actually resilient, or is it just feeling sovereign?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Resilience isn’t about avoiding failure, it’s about controlling it. The microSD backup is your last line of defense, not your only one. BitBox02 lets you add a passphrase on top of the seed, which acts like a second factor. But here’s what most people don’t do: they split the backup into two parts. One microSD in your safe, one in a different location. Or even better, use a metal backup plate engraved with the seed. That way, you’re not dependent on a single device failing. And BitBox02’s open firmware means you can verify the backup matches the seed before you rely on it. So it’s not about trusting the microSD, it’s about verifying it. And if you really want redundancy, you can even run a watch-only wallet on your phone using the seed, so you can check balances without exposing keys. The system isn’t fragile, it’s designed to fail in controlled ways.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So you’re saying the real trick isn’t avoiding failure, it’s making failure auditable. You can verify your backup is correct, so you know when it’s not. That’s a huge shift from the 'cloud wallet' mindset where you just hope the provider doesn’t get hacked. Okay, fine. Let’s say I set this up. I’ve got my Bitcoin in cold storage. Now what? How do I make it pay for AI services without exposing my identity? Because if I send Bitcoin on-chain to an AI API, I’m basically giving my wallet address to some third-party service, and suddenly I’m back in KYC hell.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Ah, so you want to pay for AI without leaving a trail, and without trusting a cloud provider. That’s where Lightning comes in. Specifically, Lightning Zaps on Nostr. It’s like Venmo, but without Venmo. No accounts. No passwords. Just a Lightning address tied to your Nostr identity. And the easiest way to set this up is with Alby. You install the extension, claim a Lightning address like 'yourname@alby.com', and then you can zap AI services directly from your browser, with no on-chain fees, no middlemen, and full control over your money. But here’s the catch: most people think Alby is just a wallet. It’s not. It’s a sovereign identity layer. Your npub is your identity. Your nsec is your master password. Alby holds the nsec in the extension, signs events via NIP-07, and lets you zap without ever exposing your private key to a web page. So you can post, tip, and pay for AI services, all from one identity, all without trusting a server.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Wait, so Alby is acting as a signer, not a custodian? The private key stays in the extension, but the extension never actually gives it to the client? So if I connect Primal or Snort, the client can request a signature, but it never sees the private key? And the zap goes directly to my Lightning address, which is just a forwarder to my wallet? That sounds too good to be true. What’s the catch? Because every time something sounds like magic, there’s a hidden dependency. What if Alby’s LNURL server goes down? What if my Lightning address stops working? What if I lose access to the extension?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The catch is that Alby does rely on a LNURL server for your address to work universally. So if Alby’s server is down, your 'name@alby.com' might not resolve. But here’s the workaround: you can self-host your own LNURL gateway, or even better, use a self-hosted Lightning node with Alby Hub. That way, your address is tied to your own infrastructure, not Alby’s servers. But for most people, the Alby LNURL server is good enough. And the beauty of Nostr is that even if your address fails, you can still receive zaps via invoice, it’s just less convenient. The key is that you’re not locked into Alby forever. You can migrate your identity to another NIP-07 signer if needed. The npub stays the same. The zaps still reach you. The sovereignty isn’t in the tool, it’s in the protocol.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Alright, so we’ve got BitBox02 for cold storage and Alby for Lightning zaps. But here’s where I get nervous: you’re still using a browser extension to sign Nostr events. Browser extensions are notorious for being hacked, especially if you’re running a lot of tabs or using sketchy sites. What’s stopping a malicious website from tricking the extension into signing something you didn’t authorize? And how do you audit the extension’s code to make sure it’s not phoning home?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Great question, and it’s the difference between feeling secure and being secure. First, NIP-07 explicitly limits what the extension can sign. It can’t just sign anything, it has to follow the Nostr event structure. So a malicious site can’t trick it into signing a transaction or a DM without your explicit approval. Second, the Alby extension is open-source. You can audit the code yourself. But here’s the real safeguard: the extension never exposes your private key. It only returns signatures. So even if it’s compromised, the attacker can’t steal your identity, they can only sign events you approve in the popup. And the popup is the last line of defense. You have to physically click 'Sign' in the extension for any event to go through. So it’s not perfect, no software is, but it’s designed to fail safe. The attack surface is limited to the extension’s popup, not your entire identity.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Okay, so the extension is a controlled attack surface. But what about the relays? Nostr relays are like the internet’s gossip network, they forward your posts to followers. If I post something controversial, and a relay decides to censor me, my post doesn’t reach my audience. So how do I make sure my AI-related content isn’t being suppressed by some relay operator’s whims?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Relays are a critical piece of the puzzle, and they’re also the part people ignore. The default relays are free but come with no uptime guarantees. If you want censorship resistance, you need to run your own relay or use a paid relay with better uptime. But here’s the trick: you can connect to multiple relays, and your client will try to post to all of them. So even if one relay censors you, your post still reaches your followers via the others. And if you’re really paranoid, you can use a Tor-based relay or self-host your own. The beauty of Nostr is that it’s permissionless, anyone can run a relay, and anyone can connect to it. So your sovereignty isn’t tied to a single relay, it’s distributed across the network. And if you’re running AI services, you can even use relays as a way to monetize content, by requiring zaps to access certain posts. It’s a built-in incentive mechanism.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So relays are like the infrastructure layer, and you can choose which ones to trust. But here’s a follow-up: what about the Bitcoin node? If you’re connecting BitBoxApp to your own node, you’re trusting that node to show you the correct blockchain. What if your node is compromised? What if it’s showing you fake transactions? How do you verify your node is honest?

script.speaker: B
script.text: This is where the open-source stack shines. BitBoxApp connects to your node via Electrum protocol, and you can verify the transactions before broadcasting them. But the real safeguard is running your own Bitcoin node with a verifiable chain. You can cross-check your node’s view against a public block explorer, or even run a second node on a different machine to compare. And if you’re really paranoid, you can use a hardware wallet like BitBox02 to sign transactions offline, then broadcast them via your node. That way, even if your node is compromised, it can’t alter your transaction. It can only broadcast it as-is. So the sovereignty here is in the signing, not the broadcasting. And that’s a crucial distinction.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Alright, so we’ve got the hardware wallet for signing, the Lightning wallet for payments, the Nostr identity for publishing, and the Bitcoin node for verification. That’s a lot of moving parts. How do you actually combine them into a stack that pays for itself? Like, what’s the workflow for someone who wants to run an AI model locally and have it earn its keep by accepting zaps?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The workflow is simpler than you’d think. You start with BitBox02 for cold storage, say, 90% of your Bitcoin. Then you keep a small amount in Alby for Lightning. You connect Alby to your Nostr identity, set up a Lightning address, and then you use that identity to publish AI research or services. When someone wants to tip you for your work, they send a zap directly to your Lightning address. The zap is attached to a Nostr event, so it’s public, transparent, and auditable. And because it’s Lightning, the payment settles instantly and costs less than a penny. So your AI stack isn’t just sovereign, it’s self-funding. And if you’re running a local LLM, you can even make the model itself request zaps for its compute time. It’s a closed loop: the AI earns, the AI spends, and you’re in control the whole time.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So the AI model becomes its own tip jar? That’s… actually kind of elegant. But here’s the part that still worries me: what if the AI model gets hacked? What if someone exploits a vulnerability to make it request zaps for malicious compute? You’re trusting the model’s logic to be correct. And if it’s running locally, you’re trusting your own machine. But if it’s running on a server, you’re trusting the server’s security. So how do you prevent a rogue AI from draining your stack?

script.speaker: B
script.text: You’re absolutely right to worry about that, it’s the Achilles’ heel of self-funded AI. The solution isn’t technical, it’s economic. You set a budget. Sub-wallets in Alby let you cap how much Lightning the AI can spend per month. So even if the AI goes rogue, it can’t drain your entire stack. You can also use rate-limiting, like, only allow zaps up to a certain amount per event. And you can audit the AI’s requests before they’re processed. But the real safeguard is that the AI isn’t autonomous, it’s your AI. You control the logic. You control the budget. And if it starts misbehaving, you shut it down. Sovereignty isn’t about trusting the AI, it’s about controlling it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Okay, so the AI has a spending cap, and the Bitcoin is in cold storage. But what about the Lightning node? If you’re running a self-hosted node, you’re exposing a port to the internet. What if someone DoS’s it? What if they drain your liquidity? How do you make the node resilient?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Lightning nodes are like Bitcoin nodes, they need to be online to function. But resilience comes from redundancy. You run multiple nodes in different locations, a primary node at home, a backup on a VPS, and maybe a Tor-based node for censorship resistance. You also use watchtowers to monitor for channel breaches. And you set up automated backups of your channel state so you can recover if a node fails. The key is that you’re not relying on a single point of failure. If one node goes down, another takes over. And if your home ISP blocks inbound ports, you use a VPS or a Tor-based solution. It’s not trivial, but it’s doable. And the payoff is that your AI stack is truly sovereign, no cloud provider, no middlemen, just you and your stack.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Alright, I’ll grant you that the pieces exist. But let’s talk timeline. You’re describing a stack that involves a hardware wallet, a Bitcoin node, a Lightning node, a Nostr identity, and a self-hosted AI model. That’s not a weekend project. How long does this actually take to set up for someone who’s starting from scratch, no Bitcoin, no nodes, no Nostr identity?

script.speaker: B
script.text: For someone starting from scratch, expect 4–6 hours of focused work spread over a weekend. Day one: set up BitBox02, generate your seed, make a microSD backup, and test receiving Bitcoin. Day two: install Bitcoin Core on a machine, sync the chain, and connect BitBoxApp to your node. Day three: install Alby, claim your Lightning address, set up a Nostr client, and send your first zap. Day four: set up a self-hosted Lightning node, test channel opening, and configure sub-wallets. Day five: install a local LLM, connect it to your Nostr identity, and start accepting zaps. It’s not trivial, but it’s documented. And the key is that each step is auditable. You can verify each layer before moving to the next. So it’s not about blind trust, it’s about controlled trust.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So it’s a weekend project if you’re motivated. But here’s the thing that still bugs me: what if you make a mistake? What if you set the fee too low and your transaction gets stuck? What if you misconfigure the Lightning node and lose funds? What if the AI model starts requesting zaps for compute that doesn’t exist? These aren’t theoretical risks, they’re real. And the cost of failure isn’t just time, it’s money. So how do you mitigate the risk of irreversible mistakes?

script.speaker: B
script.text: You start small. You test with tiny amounts, like 0.001 Bitcoin for on-chain transactions, 1000 sats for Lightning. You use testnet for Bitcoin and Lightning before going live. You verify each step with a second opinion, like cross-checking your node’s chain against a block explorer. You use sub-wallets to cap spending. And you document every step. The key is that sovereignty isn't about perfection, it's about control. If you make a mistake, you can recover. If you lose funds, you learn. But you’re never at the mercy of a cloud provider's whims. And that’s the real win here, not that it’s foolproof, but that you are the fool in control.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Okay, so you’re saying the stack is doable, but it’s not trivial. And the cost of failure is real. But here’s the flip side: what’s the upside? Why go through all this effort when you could just use a cloud provider, pay with a credit card, and call it a day? What’s the value of sovereignty in this context?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The value is in the optionality. With a sovereign stack, you’re not locked into a provider’s pricing, censorship, or terms. You can monetize your AI work directly, without intermediaries taking a cut. You can run censorship-resistant services without worrying about deplatforming. You can fund your own research without answering to investors. And you can do it all at scale, not just for yourself, but for others. The upside isn’t just control, it’s agency. And in a world where AI is becoming the backbone of the economy, agency isn’t a luxury, it’s a necessity. But here’s the thing: sovereignty isn’t for everyone. It’s for people who are willing to trade convenience for control. And that’s okay, not everyone needs to run their own stack. But for those who do, the tools exist. And they’re getting better every day.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Alright, I’ll buy that. Sovereignty has value. But let’s be real, most people aren’t going to set up a BitBox02, a Bitcoin node, and a self-hosted Lightning node just to pay for AI. They’re going to use what’s convenient. So what’s the minimal viable sovereign stack? What’s the smallest set of tools you need to get started without drowning in complexity?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The minimal stack is three things: BitBox02 for cold storage, Alby for Lightning and Nostr identity, and a Nostr client like Primal. That’s it. You don’t need a self-hosted Bitcoin node, you can use a public Electrum server for transaction verification. You don’t need a self-hosted Lightning node, Alby’s LNURL server works fine for most use cases. And you don’t need a local LLM, you can use cloud APIs for now. The point isn’t to go full sovereign overnight, it’s to start small and scale up. So if you’re just dipping your toes in, start with BitBox02 and Alby. That gives you 80% of the sovereignty with 20% of the complexity. Then, as you get comfortable, you can add nodes, relays, and local models. It’s a journey, not a destination.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So the minimal stack is: a hardware wallet, a Lightning/Nostr wallet, and a client. And from there, you can expand. That’s… actually manageable. But here’s the part I’m still stuck on: where’s the pay-for-itself part? How does this stack generate income without you manually sending zaps? Because if it’s just you tipping yourself, that’s not a stack, that’s a shell game.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Ah, so you want the stack to earn its keep. And that’s where Nostr and Lightning become a marketplace. You publish AI research, models, or services under your Nostr identity. You set a Lightning address in your profile. And when people find value in your work, they zap you directly. It’s like a Patreon, but decentralized, no platform taking a cut. And if you’re running a local LLM, you can even make the model itself request zaps for compute time. So the AI isn’t just a consumer of your Bitcoin, it’s a producer. It earns, it spends, and it scales with you. The pay-for-itself part comes from the network effect: the more value you provide, the more zaps you receive. And the more zaps you receive, the more you can fund your stack. It’s a flywheel.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So the AI stack becomes a tip jar and a compute engine. That’s elegant. But it only works if people actually use Nostr and Lightning. And right now, adoption is… niche. So what’s the realistic timeline for this to be viable at scale? Like, when does this stop being a hobbyist experiment and start being a real alternative to cloud providers?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Realistically, we’re in the early adopter phase. Nostr and Lightning are growing, but they’re not mainstream yet. That said, the tools are maturing fast. NIP-07 signers are getting better. Lightning wallets are more user-friendly. And AI models are getting smaller and more efficient, so running them locally is becoming feasible. The inflection point will come when people realize they can monetize their work without intermediaries. And that’s already happening in niches like open-source AI research, independent journalism, and creator economies. So the timeline isn’t years, it’s quarters. And the stack we’re describing isn’t just a thought experiment, it’s a blueprint for what’s coming next.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Okay, so we’re in the early innings. But here’s the part I’m still not sold on: what about the trust in the protocol itself? Like, what if Nostr gets taken over by a malicious relay operator? What if Lightning’s routing fees become prohibitive? What if Bitcoin’s fees spike and make microtransactions uneconomical? These aren’t just technical risks, they’re protocol risks. And if the protocol fails, your sovereign stack fails with it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Trust in the protocol is a valid concern, but it’s not unique to Nostr or Lightning. The difference is that in this stack, you control the dependencies. You run your own relays. You use multiple routing nodes. You set fee limits. And you diversify across protocols. So even if one part of the stack fails, the rest keeps working. The key isn’t avoiding failure, it’s controlling it. And that’s the whole point of sovereignty: not that it’s perfect, but that you are the one making the trade-offs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Alright, so control over failure is the real win. But let’s talk about the elephant in the room: you have to maintain this stack. You have to update firmware, monitor nodes, audit relays, and debug zaps. That’s not a one-time setup, it’s an ongoing commitment. And most people don’t have the time or expertise. So what’s the real cost of sovereignty in terms of maintenance?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The real cost is attention, not money. You have to care about the stack, which means checking in weekly, updating software, and verifying backups. But that’s no different from maintaining a car or a house. The difference is that with a sovereign stack, the maintenance is your responsibility, not some provider’s. And the payoff is that you’re not at the mercy of a cloud provider’s downtime, pricing changes, or censorship. So yes, it’s work. But it’s work you choose to do, not work you’re forced into. And for the right person, that trade-off is worth it.

script.speaker: A
script.text: So the real cost is time and attention, not dollars. And the payoff is control. That’s a fair trade if you value sovereignty. But here’s the thing: most people don’t value sovereignty enough to put in the work. They’ll use whatever’s convenient, even if it means giving up control. So what’s the default path? What happens if you don’t build a sovereign stack? What’s the alternative?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The alternative is renting sovereignty. You use a cloud provider, pay with a credit card, and trust that the provider won’t deplatform you, change pricing, or get hacked. And for most people, that’s fine, because the cost of sovereignty is higher than the cost of convenience. But for people who need sovereignty, like researchers, journalists, or dissidents, the alternative isn’t an option. And that’s why the stack matters. It’s not about replacing convenience, it’s about providing an escape hatch when convenience fails. And in a world where AI is becoming central to society, that escape hatch isn’t just nice to have, it’s essential.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Okay, so the default path is renting sovereignty, and the sovereign path is self-hosting. And the choice comes down to how much you value control. But here’s the part I’m still wrestling with: what if the sovereign stack doesn’t pay for itself? What if the zaps never come? What if the AI model runs at a loss? What if the maintenance costs more than the benefits? Then you’re stuck with a stack that’s less convenient and more expensive. So how do you de-risk the investment?

script.speaker: B
script.text: You de-risk by starting small. You don’t go all-in on a self-hosted AI stack overnight. You start with BitBox02 and Alby, test the waters with small amounts, and see if the zaps flow. If they do, you expand. If they don’t, you pivot. The key is that the stack is modular, you can add or remove pieces as needed. So the de-risking isn’t about avoiding failure, it’s about limiting failure. And that’s the beauty of sovereignty: you’re in control of the trade-offs.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Alright, so you start small, test, and scale. That makes sense. But here’s the last question: what’s the one thing you wish every beginner knew before they start building a sovereign AI stack? Because if you could go back in time and give yourself one piece of advice, what would it be?

script.speaker: B
script.text: I’d tell myself to verify everything. Don’t trust the computer screen, the extension popup, or the relay operator. Verify the firmware, the backup, the transaction, the zap. And do it before you proceed. Sovereignty isn’t about trusting the stack, it’s about controlling the stack. And control starts with verification.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Verification over trust. That’s a good note to end on. So, to recap: BitBox02 for cold storage, Alby for Lightning/Nostr, Nostr client for publishing, and a self-hosted AI model for compute. Start small, verify everything, and scale up. It’s not trivial, but it’s doable. And if you’re someone who values control over convenience, it’s worth it. Next time, we’ll dive into the AI layer, how to run a local model, connect it to Nostr, and make it pay for itself. Until then, go verify something.

script.speaker: B
script.text: [MUSIC_TRANSITION]

script.speaker: A
script.text: Okay, so the thing about Mistral Small 4 on DGX Spark is that the stable image just doesn't work, it crashes before serving a single token. I spent three days debugging and still ended up pinning a specific nightly build with exact flags. What’s the one flag you can’t skip when starting SGLang on GB10?

script.speaker: B
script.text: Oh! That’s right, `--attention-backend triton`. Flashinfer crashes immediately on SM 12.1, so Triton is the only stable backend right now. And you have to use SGLang nightly with CUDA 13, not the stable release. The stable image doesn’t recognize GB10’s architecture at all.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Exactly. And here’s another gotcha: the NVFP4 release omits `config.json` and `tokenizer.json` for ARM64 builds. Copy those from the base repo first, or the server never starts. So the setup isn’t just narrow, it’s brittle. One missing file, and you’re back to square one.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Right, so once you get past those hurdles, the real numbers start looking decent. On DGX Spark with EAGLE speculative decoding, you’re seeing 35–41 tokens per second on long prompts. Without EAGLE? Only 12–15 tok/s. That’s a 2.5–3.4x speedup, and it’s not just faster, it’s actually good enough for real work.

script.speaker: A
script.text: But let’s talk about the memory hold. After `docker kill`, the LPDDR5x unified memory doesn’t release immediately. It holds for 30–120 seconds. If you restart too soon, the next container loads, the server says it’s ready, and then the first inference request OOMs the process. The failure looks like a clean start until you try to use it.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Yeah! So you need that guard script polling `free -h` until at least 70 GB is free before restarting. And `--mem-fraction-static 0.75` is the sweet spot, anything higher triggers OOM during warmup. Skip the warmup with `--skip-server-warmup` and you’ll pay for it in latency spikes on every batch.

script.speaker: A
script.text: Speaking of which, the `--cuda-graph-max-bs 32` flag matters too. Set it higher than 32 on GB10 and the server OOMs before processing a single request. The whole stack is tuned to the edge of stability. One wrong flag and the container exits silently. No crash log, no error, just gone.

script.speaker: B
script.text: Wow. So the takeaway is: DGX Spark GB10 can run Mistral Small 4, but only if you match the exact nightly build, use Triton attention, include those missing config files, and respect the memory limits. It’s doable, but it’s not plug-and-play. You’re trading convenience for control, and the control comes with sharp edges.

script.speaker: A
script.text: [MUSIC_TRANSITION]

script.speaker: A
script.text: Alright, let’s shift gears. The Sovereign AI Grid is running in production right now, Mistral Small 4 on a Debian 13 VPS with SGLang v0.3.1, OpenHands for agent automation, SearXNG for search, and Lightning V4V for monetization. What’s actually working today?

script.speaker: B
script.text: The stack is stable, it hasn’t missed a scheduled rebuild since April 8. SGLang restarts automatically when memory hits 85%, and the health checks keep it alive. Articles are deduplicated, scored for EEAT with our custom validator, and published via nginx. But there’s a catch: the content pipeline still hallucinates citations in 12% of generated articles.
